title: Japanese Enzyme Baths Find Fans at Home and Abroad
paragraphs: There are few things more relaxing than taking a hot bath — and baths can be relaxing even if it's not water that you're bathing in!
Consider, for example, Japan's enzyme baths, which offer deep heat relaxation by burying you under fermenting wood and rice bran.

Enzyme baths have been getting a lot of social media attention lately as an unusual wellness treatment, with influencers posting pictures of themselves buried in large baths of ground-up wood and rice bran.

Natural fermentation allows the baths to heat up to between 65 and 80 degrees Celsius. You climb in, lie down and allow staff to bury you up to your neck — although if that feels claustrophobic, you can take your arms out.
Then things heat up very quickly, and you're soon sweating. The bathing experience doesn't take a long time, as sessions of just 15 minutes are enough to get the supposed benefits.
When you're done, you shower off the wood and rice bran, and take some time to relax and cool down with something to drink.

Enzyme baths can be great for stress relief, but it's also believed they may have a number of other benefits. These include reducing muscle and joint pain, improving circulation and cleansing the skin.

There's very little research or clinical evidence to support the benefits of enzyme bathing specifically, however. But similar heat therapies — like saunas — have been found to help with muscle pain and circulation.

It's hard to pin down the exact history of enzyme baths, but according to the Japan Enzyme Bath Association, the idea may have come from Japanese farmers using fermenting compost to keep themselves warm in winter.
Whatever their history and exact benefits, enzyme baths are finding fans both in Japan and abroad.

There are a number of clinics and spas offering them in Japanese cities like Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka, while many are getting popular in Seoul, South Korea, as well. There are even some in the US, the Czech Republic and Costa Rica!
